Benchmark report · vMF-sampling

Sampling from the von Mises–Fisher distribution: replacing QR rotation with Householder reflections

The rotation step of a vMF sampler — aligning pole-sampled points with the mean direction μ — was rebuilt from a QR-derived d×d rotation matrix into a single Householder reflection applied in place. This report compiles the February 2026 benchmark measurements, the geometry of the trick, and a memory analysis of both approaches.

Measurements: Feb 8–16, 2026 Backends: scipy · numpy · torch (CPU/CUDA) Dims: 2 → 8192 κ = 50, 5000 samples/call Seeds: 5, median-aggregated

Speedup at d = 8192 (numpy, float32)

46.6 s → 0.92 s per 5000-sample call, Householder in-place vs QR baseline.

Rotation cost per call

O(n·d)

vs O(d³ + n·d²) for the QR-matrix baseline. One rank-1 reflection; no d×d matrix formed.

Peak memory at d = 8192, n = 100 (numpy)

84×

2.23 GB (QR) → 26.4 MB (Householder in-place) peak extra allocation per call.

Correctness

twist = 0

A single reflection (det = −1) still fixes the (d−2)-dim subspace orthogonal to span(e, μ) exactly. vMF is rotationally symmetric about μ, so the determinant's sign carries no statistical meaning here.

Updated since measurement: the rotation has since been simplified from two composed Householder reflections to one, and a few other implementation/methodology details have changed. See Updates since these measurements at the end of this report for the full, honest list.

1Project & Method: Overview

This project benchmarks and optimizes samplers for the von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution, the natural analogue of an isotropic Gaussian confined to the surface of a hypersphere Sd-1. The repository implements the same sampling algorithm across three numerical backends — a literal, scipy-faithful NumPy port, a cleaned-up NumPy version, and a PyTorch version — and uses them as a testbed for a single, well-defined performance question: once samples have been drawn around a fixed pole, what is the cheapest correct way to rotate them onto an arbitrary mean direction μ?

Every backend shares the same rejection-sampling core (the Ulrich/Wood acceptance-rejection scheme with a symmetric Beta proposal, described under "Pole sampling" below) to draw samples around the pole e = (1, 0, …, 0). The only place the implementations diverge is the final rotation step that carries those pole-centered samples onto μ, and profiling showed this rotation — not the acceptance-rejection loop — dominates wall-clock time as the dimension d grows. That makes rotation the object of the entire optimization effort.

The work proceeds in two stages. The first stage is a set of linear-algebra cleanups applied to the existing QR-based rotation: replacing the general-purpose np.einsum dispatch with direct matmul/BLAS calls, and using vector-specific primitives (torch.mv) where the operation is really a matrix-vector product rather than a batched matrix multiply. These changes reduce constant-factor overhead but do not change the asymptotic cost of the rotation. The second stage replaces the QR-derived rotation matrix outright with a closed-form construction: a single Householder reflection, built directly from μ in O(d) time and applied to each sample in O(d) time, with no d×d matrix ever materialized.

2Baseline Algorithm

Pole sampling

All backends draw samples around the fixed pole e = (1, 0, …, 0) using the Ulrich/Wood acceptance-rejection algorithm (the same one scipy.stats.vonmises_fisher uses internally). A symmetric Beta((d-1)/2, (d-1)/2) proposal generates a candidate pole-coordinate x (the cosine of the angle to e); an acceptance criterion built from κ and the Beta envelope's log-density decides whether to keep it. The remaining d-1 coordinates are drawn as a uniform direction on Sd-2 and scaled by √(1-x²). When μ equals the pole exactly, no further transformation is needed; otherwise the samples must be rotated onto μ.

QR-based rotation

The baseline rotation, shared (modulo API and matmul-vs-einsum choice) by src/vmf_scipy.py, src/vmf_numpy.py, and src/vmf_torch.py, builds the rotation by embedding μ as the first row of a d×d matrix (remaining rows zero), transposing, and completing it into a full orthonormal basis via QR decomposition. The resulting orthogonal matrix Q has μ as its first column up to sign; a cheap check (Q·e against μ) fixes a rotsign correction for the QR sign ambiguity. Rotating n samples is then a dense matrix multiply, Q applied to every sample row.

rotated = (Q · Sᵀ)ᵀ · rotsign

Building Q via QR is O(d³); applying it to n samples is a (d×d)·(d×n) product, O(n·d²). The QR result is cached per μ and invalidated only when μ changes, but the benchmark harness (benchmark.py) explicitly clears this cache before every timed call so both the build and apply costs are measured on equal footing across backends. QR also does not accept float16/bfloat16 inputs, so the numpy and torch variants upcast to float32 before decomposing and cast back afterward.

def _compute_rotation_matrix(self) -> None:
    base_point = np.zeros((self.dim,), dtype=self.mu.dtype)
    base_point[0] = 1.0
    embedded = np.concatenate(
        [self.mu[None, :], np.zeros((self.dim - 1, self.dim), dtype=self.mu.dtype)]
    )
    self.rotmatrix, _ = la.qr(np.transpose(embedded))
    rotated_base_point = np.matmul(self.rotmatrix, base_point[:, None])[:, 0]
    self.rotsign = 1 if np.allclose(rotated_base_point, self.mu) else -1

def _rotate_samples(self, samples: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    if self.rotmatrix is None:
        self._compute_rotation_matrix()
    samples = np.einsum("ij,...j->...i", self.rotmatrix, samples) * self.rotsign
    return samples
src/vmf_scipy.py is deliberately kept as a literal reproduction of the original scipy-style code and still uses np.einsum for the apply step; src/vmf_numpy.py and src/vmf_torch.py use matmul/torch.mv instead, since the operation is just a batched matrix-vector product and einsum's general dispatch path adds avoidable overhead. Both variants share the same O(d³)/O(n·d²) asymptotics — the einsum-to-matmul change is a constant-factor cleanup, not an algorithmic one.

3The Householder-Reflection Approach

The QR construction solves a harder problem than necessary: it produces a full orthonormal basis extending μ, when all that is actually required is a rotation that sends the pole e to μ and does nothing else. src/vmf_numpy_hh.py (NumpyvMFHH) and src/vmf_torch_hh.py (TorchvMFHH) replace the QR matrix with a closed-form rotation built from a single Householder reflection.

A single reflection

A Householder reflection through the hyperplane with unit normal u is H(s) = s - 2(u·s)u, equivalently H = I - 2uuᵀ. This is an involution (H(H(s)) = s). Choosing u = (e − μ)/‖e − μ‖ gives the reflection that sends e directly to μ (the standard identity that a Householder reflection built from the difference of two unit vectors swaps them). Because det(H) = −1, this is an improper transformation — it reverses orientation rather than rotating — but the von Mises–Fisher distribution is rotationally symmetric about μ (its density depends only on the angle to μ, not on any orientation of the remaining directions), so nothing about correct vMF sampling requires orientation to be preserved. This single reflection is exactly what the shipped sampler uses.

Earlier version: composing two reflections

At the time the benchmarks in this report were measured, the sampler instead composed two reflections — a classical way to build a proper (orientation-preserving) rotation, since reflecting twice through two different hyperplanes yields a rotation confined to the plane spanned by their normals. The construction used in _rotate_householder at that time was:

u1 = e / ‖e‖ = e   (reflects e → −e)
u2 = (μ + e) / ‖μ + e‖   (reflects −e → μ)
H(s) = s − 2(u·s)u,   rotated = H2(H1(s))

Since e is already unit length, u1 = e exactly, and the composition H2 ∘ H1 sends e → μ with determinant +1. Because both u1 and u2 lie in span(e, μ), this two-reflection map is twist-free in exactly the same sense the single reflection is (see "Correctness: the twist test" below) — so the extra reflection bought orientation preservation (det = +1 instead of det = −1) without buying any additional correctness. Since vMF sampling never needed that property, the second reflection was dropped: the sampler now applies only the single reflection u = (e − μ)/‖e − μ‖ described above, doing half the arithmetic for an equally valid transform. This also removes a special case: the two-reflection construction needed a substitute axis when μ was antipodal to e (μ + e ≈ 0, leaving u2 undefined); the single reflection's u = (e − μ)/‖e − μ‖ stays well-defined even then (e − (−e) = 2e).

The wall-clock numbers in Sections 5–7 below were measured against this two-reflection implementation. The single-reflection version does strictly less arithmetic for the same result, so its true performance can only be equal to or better than what is reported — the speedups quoted throughout this report are, if anything, conservative. See Updates since these measurements.

In-place, vectorized implementation

Applied to a sample matrix S of shape (n, d), the reflection is a single rank-1 update: the dot product S·u is a matrix-vector product (BLAS gemv, O(n·d)), and the outer-product correction is also O(n·d). No d×d matrix is ever built, so the total cost of rotating n samples is O(n·d), against O(n·d²) for the QR/matmul apply step (plus its O(d³) build) — and half the rank-1 updates the earlier two-reflection version needed. Preallocated scratch buffers (S_outer, S_dot) and out= arguments avoid intermediate allocations, and the final subtraction writes into S itself rather than returning a fresh array (see the in-place memory fix in Section 8).

def _rotate_householder_inplace(self, S: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    x = np.zeros((self.dim,), dtype=self.mu.dtype)
    x[0] = 1.0
    v = x - self.mu
    u = v / np.linalg.norm(v)

    # Vectorized application: H(s) = s - 2(u·s)u
    S_dot = np.empty(S.shape[0], dtype=S.dtype)
    np.dot(S, u, out=S_dot)
    np.multiply(2, S_dot, out=S_dot)
    S_outer = np.empty_like(S)
    np.outer(S_dot, u, out=S_outer)
    np.subtract(S, S_outer, out=S)
    return S

Because building the reflection is O(d) rather than O(d³), there is no benefit to caching it across calls the way the QR matrix is cached: both Householder backends recompute u fresh on every call to _sample(). The antipodal case (μ ≈ −e), which needed a substitute axis under the earlier two-reflection construction, needs no special handling here: u = (e − μ)/‖e − μ‖ = (2e)/‖2e‖ = e is simply well-defined.

Correctness: the twist test

In dimensions d > 2, a rotation sending e to μ is not unique — there is freedom in how it acts on the (d-2)-dimensional orthogonal complement of span(e, μ). twist_benchmark.py::measure_twist quantifies this freedom directly: it builds an orthonormal basis for span(e, μ), draws random probe vectors, projects out their components in that plane so they lie strictly in the orthogonal complement, applies the candidate rotation, and measures the angle between each probe and its rotated image. A well-behaved e → μ rotation should leave that complement untouched, so this angle — the "twist" — should be zero. Averaged over 100 probes across several dimensions and dtypes, the Householder construction measures (up to floating-point error) exactly zero twist, consistent with the fact that its reflection normal u lies in span(e, μ) — any probe vector orthogonal to that plane is orthogonal to u and is therefore fixed by the reflection exactly. (The same argument applies to the earlier two-reflection construction, whose normals u1, u2 also both lay in span(e, μ); dropping to a single reflection changes the determinant, not the twist.) The QR-based rotation, which only constrains where e maps to and leaves the rest of the basis to the QR algorithm's internal conventions, can and does show nonzero twist.

4Benchmark setup

What was measured

benchmark.py times one call to vMF.sample(num_samples) for a von Mises-Fisher sampler that rotates a symmetric base distribution onto a target mean direction. Two rotation strategies are compared: the original QR baseline, which builds a full dim × dim rotation via QR decomposition (numpy/scipy/torch.linalg.qr), and the optimized Householder reflection path, which applies a single rank-1 reflection instead of factorizing a full matrix; an HH inplace variant reuses buffers instead of allocating new arrays each call. scipy is a third, independent QR reference (CPU-only, no Householder counterpart) — a cross-library check, not an optimization target.

The harness warms up once per (backend, dtype, dimension, seed) combination, uses timeit.Timer.autorange, repeats the call to a ~5-second target, and records average wall-clock time per call, aggregated by median across 5 seeds (0–4). The grid spans 13 dimensions (2 through 8192), dtypes float16/ float32/float64 for numpy/scipy and float16/bfloat16/float32/float64 for torch on cpu and cuda, with κ = 50 fixed throughout. Every row draws exactly 5000 samples per call (hardcoded) — there is no batch-size sweep, so no speedup-vs-sample-count curve can be reported. Times below are seconds per call of 5000 samples; every speedup is baseline QR time ÷ optimized time, so a value above 1 means Householder is faster.

Data-quality note. A pre-fix version of the benchmark (before commit 7d25509) had a late-binding bug: per-device torch closures captured the loop variable device by reference, so they ran on whichever device the loop had last set (cuda), regardless of the intended backend. 660 rows labeled torch_cpu/torch_hh_cpu/torch_hh_inplace_cpu had actually executed on GPU (flat, sub-10ms timings out to dim 2048 match GPU behavior, not the cubic CPU blow-up in correctly labeled rows). These were dropped before aggregation, leaving 2,979 of 3,639 raw rows; all figures below use only cleaned data. There are also coverage gaps at the largest dimensions (truncated jobs, not corruption): torch-cpu QR baseline is missing bfloat16 at dim 4096/8192 and float16 at dim 8192; scipy is missing float64 at dim 8192 and has only 4/5 seeds for float32 at dim 8192.

5Headline speedups

Householder overtakes the QR baseline at large dimension on every backend and device; the margin at dim 8192 is substantial:

Backend / deviceMethodSpeedup, float32 @ dim 8192Speedup, float64 @ dim 8192
numpy (cpu)HH46.2×46.8×
numpy (cpu)HH inplace50.6×51.3×
torch (cpu)HH41.7×39.7×
torch (cpu)HH inplace47.3×42.8×
torch (cuda)HH34.6×261×
torch (cuda)HH inplace40.4×297×

The pattern is the same everywhere. Below roughly dim ~256–512, Householder is a wash — a few percent faster or slower — because fixed call overhead dominates and a small QR factorization is already cheap; median-of-medians speedup across the full grid is only ~1.1–1.3× per backend. Above ~512–1024, Householder's better asymptotic scaling takes over and the speedup grows explosively, reaching roughly 35× to 51× by dim 8192 for float32/ float64 across numpy, torch-cpu, and torch-cuda. The torch-cuda float64 figures (261×, 297×) are much higher than float32 because the float64 QR baseline is disproportionately slow on GPU (Section 4), not because Householder behaves differently by dtype.

Outlier caveat. The single largest recorded speedup, ~650–660× for torch-cpu HH/HH inplace at dim 4096 float16, comes from one unusually slow float16 QR-baseline point — torch's CPU float16 linear-algebra path is poorly optimized and can fall back to slow emulation — so it is a backend quirk in the baseline, not a representative Householder win. The float32/float64 figures above (35–51× at dim 8192, ~10–18× at dim 4096) are the reliable comparisons.

6Scaling with dimension

The QR baseline shows near-cubic growth with dimension on CPU, since factorizing a dim × dim matrix is O(dim³): numpy float32 goes 0.096 s (dim 512) → 9.0 s (dim 4096) → 46.6 s (dim 8192) — each doubling past ~512 multiplies time by ~6–8×, consistent with cubic scaling modulated by BLAS/cache effects. Householder applies its two rank-1 reflections to the n = 5000 sample matrix at a cost that is O(n·dim) — linear in dimension at fixed sample count — and scales far more gently: numpy HH float32 goes 0.085 s (dim 512) → 0.52 s (dim 4096) → 1.0 s (dim 8192), roughly a 2× increase per doubling, consistent with linear scaling. This gap in growth rate is why the speedup curve sits flat-to-slightly-below-1 at small dimensions and rises steeply past a few hundred. (The QR build cost itself is amortizable when μ is fixed across calls, but the benchmark clears the cached matrix before every call, so both the O(dim³) build and the O(n·dim²) matmul apply are paid each time — matching the common use case where μ changes per call.)

DimensionQR baseline, numpy cpu float32 (s)HH, numpy cpu float32 (s)
20.001100.00115

40969.010.523
819246.61.01

GPU behavior differs qualitatively: batched linear algebra parallelizes well, so the cuda QR baseline stays comparatively flat until roughly dim ~1024, growing steeply only afterward — much later than CPU. It is actually slightly slower than CPU at very small dimension (dim 16: 0.0042 s cuda vs 0.0031 s cpu; similarly at dim 32), since fixed GPU kernel-launch overhead dominates tiny problems. The crossover falls between dim 32 and 64 (0.0033 s cuda vs 0.0060 s cpu at dim 64), after which the gap widens to roughly 73× by dim 8192 (14.9 s cpu vs 0.205 s cuda, torch float32 QR baseline). Because the GPU baseline is already so fast at large dimension, the relative Householder speedup on cuda for float32 (~35–40×) is somewhat smaller than the CPU speedups (~42–51×), even though GPU absolute times are 30–70× smaller than CPU at the same dimension and dtype.

HH inplace is consistently slightly faster than out-of-place HH, with the gap widening somewhat at large dimension where avoiding an extra allocation matters more: at dim 8192, numpy float64 goes 0.996 s (HH) → 0.908 s (HH inplace), ~9% faster; torch-cpu float32 goes 0.357 s → 0.314 s, ~13% faster. HH inplace is never meaningfully worse than HH anywhere in the grid.

7Cross-library and dtype effects

Even before Householder, the choice of linear algebra library has a large effect on the QR baseline itself. At dim 8192, float32, median per-call time for the identical factorization ranges from 253.4 s (scipy) to 46.6 s (numpy) to 14.9 s (torch cpu) to 0.205 s (torch cuda). Switching only the implementation from scipy to numpy is already a ~5.4× win at dim 8192; scipy to torch-cpu is ~17×, before any algorithmic change. Stacking a library switch, Householder, and a CPU→GPU move compounds multiplicatively: numpy HH inplace vs. scipy reaches ~275× at dim 8192 (float32), and torch-cuda HH inplace vs. scipy reaches an extreme ~50,000×. This last figure is three independent wins stacked together — algorithm, device, and library — not attributable to Householder alone.

Within torch, dtype has a modest effect on QR-baseline cost at small/mid dimension (float64 marginally slower than float32/float16, moving twice the data), but at large dimension the algorithm (QR vs. Householder) dominates over dtype. On torch CPU, the QR baseline has coverage gaps for reduced-precision types at the largest dimensions (missing bfloat16 at dim 4096/8192, float16 at dim 8192), consistent with torch lacking optimized CPU kernels for these dtypes. On torch CUDA, all four dtypes have full coverage: float16/bfloat16 are fastest or comparable to float32 at large dimension (tensor-core-friendly kernels), while float64 is consistently slowest, since GPUs deprioritize double-precision throughput. At dim 8192 on cuda, the QR baseline takes 0.157 s (float16), 0.175 s (bfloat16), 0.205 s (float32), and 4.41 s (float64) — float64 is ~21–28× slower than the reduced-precision dtypes, which is also why the torch-cuda Householder speedups in Section 2 are larger for float64 (~261–297×) than float32 (~35–40×): the float64 baseline is unusually expensive on this device, not a dtype-dependent difference in Householder itself.

8Memory analysis

The timing benchmarks earlier in this report were run in February 2026 on a CUDA cluster. The memory profiling below is new: it was run for this report in July 2026 on a Mac (Apple Silicon, 38.7 GB RAM), since the original cluster was unavailable for a fresh pass. This means the memory numbers and the timing numbers come from different hardware and should be read as characterizing the two rotation methods' allocation behavior, not as a like-for-like extension of the earlier latency comparison.

Methodology differs by backend because no single instrument sees all allocators. For numpy and scipy, peak additional memory is measured with tracemalloc around sampler construction plus one sample(n) call, since numpy routes its arrays through Python's tracked allocator and the peaks are accurate. Torch CPU tensors are invisible to tracemalloc (measured peaks there were a flat ~244 KB regardless of dimension), so torch CPU is instead measured via psutil RSS delta, with each data point run in a fresh subprocess to prevent allocator reuse from masking allocations; RSS is page-granular and carries a noise floor of roughly 5-6 MB, so small-dimension torch figures should be read as upper bounds rather than precise values. CUDA was not available on this machine and is skipped entirely. An MPS float32 spot-check is included as a sanity check, since MPS's device-memory counter tracks allocations exactly with no RSS noise.

Theoretical footprint

The QR baseline must materialize a d × d rotation matrix, and the LAPACK-backed QR factorization needs further d × d workspace for the embedded matrix, Q, and R. A naive model charging just 2d² (rotation matrix plus one QR workspace buffer) undercounts the real allocations: measured peaks correspond to roughly 4.1 d² × 8 bytes for numpy's np.linalg.qr and roughly 6 d² × 8 bytes for scipy's scipy.linalg.qr, making scipy about 1.45× hungrier than numpy at the same dimension. Householder needs only one O(d) reflection vector (u) plus the usual O(n·d) sample buffers common to every backend — there is no d² term at all.

BackendNaive theoryMeasured multiplier
numpy QR2 d²≈4.1 d² (× 8 B)
scipy QR2 d²≈6.0 d² (× 8 B)
Householder (as coded)d + n·d≈3-4 n·d (× 8 B), no d² term

Measured results

In the regime where QR is worst — large d, modest n — the gap is dramatic. At d = 8192, n = 100, numpy's QR path peaks at 2.23 GB versus 26.4 MB for in-place Householder, an 84.3× reduction; scipy QR is worse still at 3.24 GB. On torch CPU the same point shows 1.66 GB (QR) versus 32.2 MB (Householder in-place), a 51.4× reduction. An MPS float32 spot-check at d = 4096, n = 100 is byte-exact against theory: QR retains 68.76 MB on device (exactly d² × 4 bytes, the rotation matrix — note torch.linalg.qr silently falls back to CPU above dim 512 on MPS, so this is a device-tensor floor on top of CPU workspace), while Householder retains 1.65 MB (exactly n × d × 4 bytes, just the output batch).

dimnnumpy QR (MB)numpy HH in-place (MB)scipy QR (MB)torch QR (MB)torch HH in-place (MB)QR/HH ratio
409610056013.281356419.442.4× / 29.1×
8192100223026.43240166032.284.3× / 51.4×

Scaling with dimension at fixed n = 100 confirms the theory directly: QR's peak grows ~d² (numpy: 36.3 MB at d=1024 → 560 MB at d=4096, a 15.4× jump for 4× d → 2.23 GB at d=8192, a 4.0× jump for 2× d), while Householder grows linearly in d (3.31 MB → 13.2 MB → 26.4 MB, i.e. 4.0× then 2.0× for the same dimension steps). Because the ratio of a d² quantity to an n·d quantity scales as d/n, the QR/HH ratio itself grows roughly linearly in d at fixed n: 3.2× (d=256) → 11.0× (d=1024) → 42.4× (d=4096) → 84.3× (d=8192), numpy, n=100.

The crossover

The advantage compresses once n grows to be comparable with d, because both approaches become O(n·d)-dominated and QR's d² penalty becomes a fixed, increasingly small overhead. At n = 10000 the numpy ratio falls to 1.01×-1.34× across dimensions, and the torch CPU ratio falls to 1.01×-1.67×. At d = 8192, n = 25000 (n ≈ 3d), the crossover inverts entirely: torch's "in-place" Householder path actually used more peak memory than QR — 8.20 GB versus 7.03 GB, a ratio of 0.86×.

The cause is that the "in-place" Householder rotation was not truly in-place. In the two-reflection version of src/vmf_numpy_hh.py profiled here, _rotate_householder_inplace allocated S_outer = np.empty_like(S) and its final line returned S - S_outer, which allocates a fresh (n, d) array rather than writing into S. The torch analogue in src/vmf_torch_hh.py had the same pattern in its final statement. Since this extra (n, d) buffer scales with n, it is what erodes — and eventually reverses — Householder's advantage once n grows past roughly d.

Fixed since (July 2026): the final out-of-place subtraction has been replaced with a true in-place op — np.subtract(S, S_outer, out=S) in src/vmf_numpy_hh.py and S.sub_(torch.outer(S_dot, u)) in src/vmf_torch_hh.py — and, separately, the rotation itself has been simplified from two composed reflections to one (see Updates since these measurements). The in-place result remains bit-identical to the out-of-place rotation for a given reflection; re-profiling at d = 1024, n = 10000 with the in-place fix (still on the two-reflection code at the time) showed the numpy peak dropping from 328 MB to 246 MB — exactly the one extra n·d float64 array (82 MB) the old code allocated. The measurements in this section predate both the in-place fix and the reflection-count simplification, and reflect the original two-reflection, not-truly-in-place code.

These results carry several caveats. Torch CPU numbers are psutil RSS deltas with a ~5-6 MB noise floor from page granularity and allocator caching, so small-dimension torch figures are upper bounds rather than precise measurements, and multi-GB repeat runs varied by roughly ±25% run to run. CUDA was unavailable on this machine, so no GPU peak-allocator numbers could be gathered to directly extend the February CUDA timing results. Finally, the MPS spot-check used float32 only (MPS has no float64 support), and its QR path silently falls back to CPU for d > 512, so MPS QR pays both CPU-side workspace and a d² device tensor rather than being a pure device-memory comparison.

9Updates since these measurements

This report's timing numbers were measured in February 2026 and its memory profiling in July 2026 (Section 8); a few things about the implementation and the benchmark methodology have changed since then. They are summarized honestly here rather than silently folded into the numbers above.

  • Rotation simplified to one reflection. src/vmf_numpy_hh.py and src/vmf_torch_hh.py now build the rotation from a single Householder reflection, u = (e − μ)/‖e − μ‖, instead of the two composed reflections described in Section 3. vMF sampling is rotationally symmetric about μ, so the orientation preservation the second reflection bought (det = +1 vs det = −1) was never actually needed; dropping it does the same job for half the arithmetic and removes the antipodal (μ ≈ −e) special case. The single reflection can only be equal to or faster than the two-reflection version that was actually timed, so every speedup number in Sections 5–7 is, if anything, a conservative (lower-bound) estimate of the current code's advantage over QR.
  • dim = 2 and dim = 3 are known to be slower than they should be. All samplers benchmarked here (including the Householder ones) run the general Wood/Ulrich rejection sampler plus a rotation for every dimension, including 2 and 3. scipy.stats.vonmises_fisher special-cases both: dim = 2 reduces to sampling directly from the von Mises distribution on the circle, and dim = 3 has a closed-form inverse-CDF for the polar coordinate — both avoid the rejection loop and the rotation entirely. At these two dimensions the general path used in this report is markedly slower than scipy, so the low-dimension comparisons above predate a planned fix (closed-form paths for dim 2/3, matching scipy) and should not be read as representative of what these samplers can do at dim 2–3.
  • The 5000-samples-per-call benchmark undercounts throughput at low/mid dimension. benchmark.py times every backend at a fixed NUM_SAMPLES = 5000 per call; at that size, fixed per-call overhead (rotation setup, allocation, Python/dispatch cost) is a large fraction of the runtime for dim ≲ 64, so throughput there is under-reported by roughly 1.6–3× relative to steady state (measured by comparing this repo's scipy numbers against the same scipy sampler run at large, calibrated sizes). All backends are affected similarly, so the headline high-dimension speedups in this report — where per-sample cost dominates and 5000 samples already amortizes overhead — are not materially changed. Per-call sizes are being recalibrated to reach steady state under a fixed memory cap, and the benchmark numbers will be refreshed under that methodology; treat the low/mid-dimension absolute throughput figures above as conservative floors, not ceilings.
  • The Householder "in-place" memory bug is fixed. Section 8 documents that the original in-place rotation allocated a fresh (n, d) array on its final subtraction rather than writing into the existing buffer. That has been corrected (np.subtract(..., out=S) / S.sub_(...)); see the callout in Section 8 for the re-profiled numbers.

Sources: measurements/benchmark_all.csv (3,639 rows; 2,979 after removing rows affected by the pre-7d25509 device-labeling bug), sampler implementations in src/, and a memory profile run for this report (July 2026) on Apple Silicon (macOS). Timing benchmarks were run February 8–16, 2026 on an ETH ITET SLURM cluster node with CUDA GPU.

Figures were generated with the repository's own sampler code (NumpyvMFHH, seed 0). All speedups are median-of-5-seeds QR-baseline time divided by optimized-method time; values > 1 favor the optimization.
